title: Trump, Xi and Putin Hold Historic Talks in China
paragraphs: US President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin have held their first-ever three-way summit, presenting themselves as partners in promoting peace but offering few concrete commitments.
The leaders met in Shenzhen, China, on November 19, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. Their talks lasted more than an hour.
The leaders emphasized their countries' roles as World War II victors and their shared responsibility for maintaining international security.

Their joint "peace declaration" called for reforms to the United Nations, increased oil supplies and dialogue to reduce nuclear risks. However, it did not explain the type and extent of the UN reforms the leaders agreed to.
The statement also made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the US-led war in Iran.
Trump described the gathering as "really making history" and presented it as a starting point for tackling international problems.

He said he and Xi agreed that Iran should fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global energy supplies, and must not obtain a nuclear weapon. However, there was no sign that he secured commitments from either Xi or Putin to help resolve the Iran conflict.
For Putin, the meeting offered an opportunity to present Russia as a global power equal to the US and China. It was his first appearance at an APEC summit since 2017.

The three sides also agreed that state officials should enjoy immunity from prosecution, and criticized the International Criminal Court (ICC). Putin faces an ICC arrest warrant for alleged war crimes in Ukraine, while the US opposes its warrant against former Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

For Xi, hosting the event reinforced China's growing diplomatic influence. Beijing wanted to present itself as a power promoting peace while steering the meeting away from specifics, according to Ruby Osman, a policy adviser at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change.
Xi expressed optimism about the potential for future cooperation.
"As long as dialogue does not stop, doors remain open, there is hope for peace," he said.
